docs.title: BIMopen user manual
docs.text:
BIMopen is an open-source application for building information modelling (BIM). You model the building with walls, doors, windows, floors, roofs, stairs and rooms, and the drawings come from the model: plans, sections, elevations, 3D views, schedules and sheets are views of the same model and change together when you edit it.

BIMopen runs on the desktop (Linux, Windows, macOS) and in a web browser, and it can be driven from a command line and by AI agents over MCP. Its interface speaks six languages: Italian, English, German, French, Spanish and Arabic, the last one written from right to left.

The BIMopen window with the sample house in the 3D view

docs.title: How this manual is organised
docs.text:
Chapter What it covers Getting started Installing and starting BIMopen, the sample project, and a first small house from an empty project to a sheet The interface The BIMopen style: the rail and the tool panel, the top bar, the command search, the options strip, the element panel, the Project Index, the views strip, the drawing area, the status bar and how to move around in the views Interface styles The Classic style, and touch mode on touch monitors, tablets and phones Projects and files Opening, saving, exporting and importing projects Selecting and modifying Selecting elements and the Modify tools Walls, doors and windows The building envelope and its openings Floors, roofs, stairs and components Floors, roofs, stairs, railings, curtain walls and placed components Views and graphics Plans, sections, elevations, 3D views and how they are drawn Annotation and 2D details Dimensions, text, tags, rooms, areas and 2D details Sheets, schedules and printing Sheets, schedules, printing and project settings Command line and MCP Typing commands, bimopen-cli and the MCP server for agents Keyboard shortcuts Every key and typed shortcut Troubleshooting What to do when something does not work as expected

The chapters from Projects and files to Sheets, schedules and printing are being written area by area: each one is completed when the features it describes have been checked one by one through the interface. Until then they list what they will contain.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• The manual describes and pictures the BIMopen interface style, the one BIMopen starts in. Interface styles shows the Classic style and touch mode, which run the same commands.
  • Names of the interface are written in bold, as they appear on the screen in English: Create on the rail, Wall tile, Properties tab.
  • A path through the interface is written with arrows: Create ▸ Build ▸ Wall means Create on the rail, then the Build group of the tool panel, then its Wall tile.
  • Keys are written like Ctrl+Z; a shortcut typed at the keyboard, letter by letter, is written in capitals, like WA.
  • Commands typed at the command line, and their output, are written like this. Points are x,y in metres.
  • Notes, tips and warnings are set apart:

Note

A note adds something worth knowing.

Tip

A tip shows a quicker or better way.

Warning

A warning tells you about something that can lose work or give a wrong result.

docs.title: What this manual describes
docs.text:
This manual describes BIMopen as it is today, and only what has been tried in the program. When a feature is not described yet, it may still exist: the roadmap lists what is available and what is planned. The whole manual is also a PDF, one per language: the last entry of the navigation, PDF, downloads it.

BIMopen is free software under the MIT or Apache 2.0 licence.

docs.title: Annotation and 2D details
docs.text:
This chapter describes dimensions and constraints, text notes, tags, rooms and areas with their colour schemes, legend views, and the 2D drawing tools: detail lines, regions, detail components, repeating details, insulation and free 2D views. Annotations belong to the view they are made in: a dimension placed in a plan does not appear in another plan.

Before each click, every tool shows what it would make where the cursor is: the dimension with its value, the note's box, the tag on the element under the cursor, the region a room or area would fill, the line, region, component or insulation being drawn.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: Annotations ▸ Dimension holds the dimension tools: Aligned, Linear, Angular, Radial, Arc length, and the spot dimensions Spot Elevation, Spot Coordinate and Spot Slope. They work in plans, sections, elevations, free 2D views and legends. Pick the dimension type in the type selector while the tool is on; Type Parameters changes the type, and with it every dimension of that type.

docs.title: Aligned and linear dimensions
docs.text:
With Aligned, the options bar offers which part of a wall is picked (Wall centerlines, Wall faces, Center of Core, Faces of Core) and what a click picks:

  • References: click references one after the other (wall faces or centre lines, grids, door and window edges, detail lines, the edges of legend symbols), then click an empty spot to place the dimension line there. While you choose, the string follows the cursor. Press TAB over a wall to step through its references.
  • Entire Walls: one click dimensions a whole wall. Options opens the automatic dimensioning options: Openings with their Centers or both Widths, Intersecting Walls and Intersecting Grids. A grid that falls on a wall end adds no witness line.
Aligned: pick two references, then place the line

Linear measures along the horizontal or the vertical of the view, between points such as wall ends: where you place the line decides which, and the space bar switches between the two.

Angular measures the angle between two walls, grids or lines that meet; more lines through the same point make a string of angles, each with its value; the last click picks the sector. Radial and Arc length dimension an arc: click it, then where the dimension goes.

An ordinate type has Ordinate Dimension Settings in its type parameters: Edit… opens a dialog with the Text Orientation (Aligned with the witness lines or Horizontal), the Text Location (In line with the witness line or Above the witness line), the Origin Visibility, the Origin Marker (Zero value, Circle or the type's Tick Mark) and the Dimension Line Style (Continuous or None, which leaves only the witness lines and ticks).

docs.title: Changing a dimension
docs.text:
• Select a dimension and click its value: Dimension Text opens. Use Actual Value keeps the measure and adds text above, below, before or after it; Replace with text shows words instead (a number is refused).
  • Drag the blue control under the text to move it away from the line; dragged back near the line, it snaps into place. Text moved far away gets an arc leader to its segment; Leader on the options bar removes it.
  • Selection: Dimensions ▸ Witness Lines ▸ Edit Witness Lines: click elements to add witness lines, click an existing witness line to remove it, then click an empty spot to finish. Each witness line of a selected dimension has a control in its middle: right-click it ▸ Move Witness Line, then click the new reference; or ▸ Delete Witness Lines. The control at the element's end of a witness line drags its gap from the element; near another witness line's gap it takes the same.
  • Select an element the dimension measures and click a value next to it: type a new distance and press Enter, and the element moves: a wall, a grid, a door or window (along its wall) or a detail line.
Dimension Text

The type sets the tick (diagonal, filled arrow or dot), the extensions of the dimension and witness lines (Witness line control: a gap to the element, or Fixed to Dimension Line with its Witness Line Length), the Dimension Line Snap Distance (while placing, the line snaps at multiples of it from what it measures; 0 turns it off), the Line Weight and Tick Mark Line Weight, the Centerline Symbol, Centerline Pattern and Centerline Tick Mark (Default is the type's tick) of witness lines to centre lines, the colour, the text size, offset, background, bold, italic and underline, the units (Units Format opens Format: Use project settings, or a unit with its rounding, which may be Custom with a Increment factor, its symbol and options), and for linear dimensions the Dimension String Type: Continuous, Baseline (stacked values from the first reference) or Ordinate (values from the first reference along one line). Show Opening Height writes the height of a door or window under the width measured jamb to jamb. Radial types can drop the R prefix and their centre mark (Center Marks, with its size). With arrows, a segment too short for them has them outside, and the line runs on past them by Flipped Dimension Line Extension. Annotations ▸ Dimension ▸ Dimension Types opens the type parameters of each family's current type, to set before dimensioning.

A selected baseline string shows a flip control at its origin: click it, or press the space bar, to measure from the other end. Baseline Offset in its properties sets the distance between its lines on paper.

docs.title: Temporary dimensions
docs.text:
Select an element and temporary dimensions show its distances to the nearest references parallel to it: walls, grids, levels, reference planes, floor edges, room separation lines and detail lines. They show for every category in every view the element is drawn in: plans, sections, elevations and 3D views, where they lie on the element's level. A selected level shows its distances to the levels above and below it, in a section or an elevation.

Temporary dimensions of a selected wall

Click a value, type a new one and press Enter to move the element: a length takes a unit of its own (2.5 m), and a formula starts with = (=8000/2). Click the dimension symbol beside it to make it permanent.

Each witness line has a blue control. Drag the one on the reference onto any other reference to measure from there; or right-click it ▸ Move Witness Line, then click the new reference. A click on a control steps through the references of the same object: a wall's centerline, its faces, its core faces and its core centerline. The element remembers the references chosen, for each view, and they follow when the reference moves; right-click ▸ Reset References goes back to the nearest ones.

With several elements selected none are shown, and the options bar offers Activate Dimensions to show them for all the selected elements.

While a component, a door or a window is placed, temporary dimensions show its distances to the nearest references; Tab steps to the next ones. Rest the pointer for a moment: the element waits while the pointer goes to one of its values, and a click on the value types the distance it goes at. While drawing, the length and the angle are shown; Rotate shows the angle as an angular dimension, and an angle typed turns the selection.

Project ▸ Additional settings ▸ Temporary Dimensions sets where walls measure from (Centerline, Faces, Center of Core, Core Faces) and doors and windows (Centerline or Openings), for the whole project. The same dialog sets the text of every temporary dimension, for the application: from 8 to 20 pt (8 at first), on a transparent or an opaque background. Beside the settings a preview shows three walls measured as chosen; the Preview switch in the dialog's header hides it, the dialog keeping its size, and the choice is kept.

Temporary Dimensions settings

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Select a dimension: a padlock is shown on each segment. Click it to lock the segment: the distance then holds when either element moves, and a move that would break it is refused. Click it again, or right-click it ▸ Toggle Lock, to unlock; right-click ▸ Show Related selects the two elements the lock ties. A string of two segments or more shows EQ: click it and the references become equally spaced, and stay so when one of them moves. Equality display in the properties shows the values instead of EQ.

Padlocks and EQ on a selected dimension

Selecting an element a constraint holds shows the constraint as blue dashed lines, unless the category Constraints is hidden in Visibility and Graphics. Deleting a dimension that holds a constraint asks what to do: OK deletes the dimension and keeps the constraint; Delete Elements deletes both. Modify ▸ Align with its padlock closed is a constraint too.

docs.title: Spot dimensions
docs.text:
• Spot Elevation: in a plan, click a floor, a roof or the level; in a section, any point. The value is in metres with its sign.
  • Spot Coordinate: the north and east coordinates of a point in a plan.
  • Spot Slope: the slope of a roof pitch in a plan, or of a sloped line in a section, with an arrow pointing down.
Spot elevations in a section

The options bar offers Leader and, with a leader, Shoulder: with no leader one click places the spot; with a leader, click the point and then the text; with a shoulder, the point, the bend and the text. While you hover, the value shows at the cursor. For spot elevations it also offers Relative Base: (for a type whose Elevation Origin is Relative) and, in plans, Display Elevations:: the actual elevation, the top, the bottom, or both. For spot slopes, Slope Representation: draws an Arrow or, in sections, a Triangle.

A selected spot has grips at its point, its shoulder and its text: drag the point and the spot measures what is there. A spot on a floor or a roof is deleted with it. While placing a spot, Esc lets go of the one half placed; a second Esc ends the tool.

The spot type sets Elevation Indicator, Top Indicator and Bottom Indicator (the top or bottom indicator, then the elevation's, then the value; each one's … as Prefix/Suffix puts it after the value instead), the Symbol, Include Elevation and the North/South Indicator and East/West Indicator of coordinates (with Indicator as Prefix/Suffix), and the Leader Line Length and Slope Direction (Down or Up) of slopes.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Annotations ▸ Text ▸ Text (TX): click where the note goes and type; Enter starts a new line. A click gives a note that does not wrap; dragging gives it a width, and the words wrap in it. Clicking elsewhere finishes the note, and Esc ends the tool. Tab while typing moves the text to the next tab stop. The text size is on paper: the note keeps its printed size at any view scale.

The Format panel sets, before placing or on a selected note:

  • the leader: No Leader, One Segment (click the tip, then the note), Two Segments (tip, elbow, note) or Curved;
  • the alignment, left, centre or right, and Bold, Italic and Underline (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+U while typing or on the selected notes), which apply to the whole note;
  • on a selected note, Add Left Straight Leader and the other three leader buttons, and Remove Last Leader;
  • Left Attachment and Right Attachment (Top, Middle, Bottom): where the leaders meet the note; chosen while placing, they stay for the next notes.
  • Paragraph Format: the paragraphs as a list, with Bullets, Numbers, Lowercase letters or Uppercase letters; the text of each item starts at the first tab stop, and wrapped lines are indented by one.

Near the line of another note's corner, a new note snaps to it, and a dashed line shows it.

On a selected note, drag the cross to move the box (the leader tips stay), the round side controls to change its width, and the rotation control to turn it. A grip in the middle of each leader makes an elbow when dragged, or bends a curved leader. Double-click inside it to edit the words. Its properties include Arc Leaders, Left Attachment and Right Attachment, and Keep Readable, which never shows it upside down. The text type sets the colour (of text, border and leaders), the background (Opaque masks what is behind), Show Border with its offset, the leader arrowhead, the Line Weight of the border and leaders, the size, the Tab Size (12.7 mm), bold, italic and underline. The small Text Types button of the Text panel opens Type Parameters, where Duplicate… makes a new text type.

A selected note with its leader and controls

Annotations ▸ Text ▸ Find/Replace finds words in the notes of the current selection, the current view or the whole project (Scope:), with options for case and whole words. Find All lists the matches with the view they are in; Find Next, or a click on a row, selects that note and shows its whole text under Context. Replace changes the match highlighted (the first when none is), Replace All every one, and Close closes the dialog. On selected notes it is also under Tools of their tab.

Find/Replace

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text: Annotations ▸ Symbol ▸ Symbol (SY) places a 2D annotation symbol in a plan, a section, a free 2D view or a legend: a North Arrow, a Centerline Symbol, a Flow Arrow, a Target or a Revision Delta, the last two with a text of their own. The symbol follows the cursor before the click; the space bar turns it a quarter, or Rotation on the options bar sets its angle. With Number of leaders: above zero, the click places the symbol and the next clicks put the ends of its leaders. The type sets the symbol's size on paper and its leaders' arrowhead; Duplicate… in Type Parameters makes a new one.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Annotations ▸ Tag ▸ Tag by Category (TG): hover an element (a door, window, wall, room or area) and click to tag it. The options bar sets Horizontal or Vertical, the Leader and its length; the space bar switches the orientation, while placing or on a selected tag. Door and window tools have Tag on Placement, so each new door or window comes with its tag.

Tag by Category: the preview, then the tag

Tag All opens Tag All Not Tagged: tick the categories, the tag type of each, the leader and the orientation, for all the elements of the view or only the selected ones; only elements with no tag get one.

Tag All

With a leader, Attached End ends it on the element; Free End ends it where you clicked, and a selected tag shows a grip to drag that end anywhere (Leader End in the properties switches between the two). A tag lines up with the other tags of its kind while you place it or drag it: near the line of another tag's centre it snaps to it, and a dashed line shows it. Tags hidden in the view (Visibility and Graphics) are turned on when you tag, and the message says so.

Double-click a tag to edit what it shows: a door's mark or a wall's type mark in place; a room's or area's number and name together in Edit Label Values. A tag takes another type of its own category from the type selector, and Pick New Host (Host panel) moves it to another element of the same category. Room label types choose whether they show the number, the area and the volume. A room or area label set to Pattern keeps an angle: it turns with Rotate, and the space bar lines it up with each wall near it in turn (Rotation in its properties). Deleting a room's label leaves the room, and the message says so.

docs.title: Rooms
docs.text:
Home ▸ Rooms and Areas ▸ Room (RM), then click inside a region enclosed by walls or room separators: the room fills it, around free-standing walls too. In the options bar:

  • Upper Limit and Offset: the room reaches that level plus the offset (4000 mm by default); a higher level gives a room over several storeys, such as an atrium;
  • Tag on Placement, on by default, with the tag's orientation and leader;
  • Room: New, or a room that is not placed, to put it back;
  • Highlight Boundaries: walls and separators that bound rooms turn orange, and the warning lists them.
Room: the region it fills, then the room and its tag

A room placed in open space is kept with a warning, and takes its shape once the space is closed; a second room in a region already taken is marked Redundant Room and not counted twice. A number another room already has, a room lower than the computation height (1200 mm) and a base above it are warned about too, and so is a room separator drawn over another.

Walls bound the rooms of a level when they stand at its computation height: 1200 mm while Automatic Room Computation Height is ticked in the level's properties, otherwise its Computation Height.

A section shows the rooms it cuts when they are selected or under the cursor (TAB reaches a room behind other elements). A room selected there has an arrow at its top and one at its base: drag them to change its Limit Offset and Offset at Base.

Room Separator draws lines that split a space into rooms without walls. A wall bounds rooms while its Room Bounding property is on. Floors and roofs above cap the room's volume.

Deleting a room removes it from the plan but keeps it in the project, Not Placed, with its data; its tags go with it. Deleting a room label leaves the room. A room label dragged out of its room asks whether to Move to Room.

Rooms show through their tags. In Visibility and Graphics, Rooms has Interior Fill and Datum (the cross lines). Settings ▸ Area and Volume Computations opens on Computations: the room boundary at the wall finish, centre, core layer or core centre, and Areas and Volumes to compute volumes too (by default only areas; the volume is always measured to the wall finish). Its second tab is Area Schemes.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text:
Areas belong to an area scheme: Gross Building (which cannot be deleted) and Rentable come with every project, and Area Schemes ▸ New adds more.

  1. Rooms and Areas ▸ Area ▸ Area Plan: pick the scheme and the levels. Answer Yes to draw area outlines along the exterior walls, No to draw them yourself.
  2. Area ▸ Area Outline: draw the outlines, or pick walls; with the area rules on, an exterior wall of a gross plan gives its outer face.
  3. Area ▸ Area: click inside the outlines. The area is tagged when placed; Tag ▸ Area Label tags it later. Placed where no outlines close a region, the area is kept with a warning and takes its shape once they do; a second area in a region is Redundant Area.

Deleting an area leaves it in the project, not placed, without its tags; Area: in the options bar of the Area tool lists the areas not placed, to put one back with a click.

docs.title: Colour schemes
docs.text:
A colour scheme fills the rooms or areas of a plan (and the rooms a section cuts) by a value (name, number, department, area type) or by ranges of area. Set it in the plan's Color Scheme property; (none) turns it off. Settings ▸ Color Schemes (Edit Color Scheme) creates and duplicates schemes and edits the title, the parameter, the values with their colour and visibility, their order and the ranges. Apply keeps the changes and sets the scheme of the view with the dialog open. Color scheme location, a view property, draws the fills in the Background (under the model) or in the Foreground (over the model, under the annotations).

Edit Color Scheme

Rooms and Areas ▸ Legend places the legend of the plan's scheme: a swatch and a label for each value. Its Values displayed are By view (those in the plan) or All, and Columns flows the swatches into several columns. A plan can have several legends; deleting one leaves the scheme.

Rooms by colour, and the legend

docs.title: Legend views
docs.text:
Views ▸ Legends ▸ Legend opens New Legend View: a name and a scale. The legend opens and is listed under Legends in the Project Index. Annotations ▸ Component ▸ Legend Component places the symbol of a type: in the options bar, the type, the View it is seen from (a wall in plan or section; a floor or roof in section or plan; a door, window or component in plan, front or back) and the Host Length, the piece of wall a door or window sits in. Legend components draw at the legend's detail, can be moved and dimensioned (the edges of doors, windows and components; walls, floors and roofs are not), and are not counted by schedules. Text, detail lines and regions work as in a free 2D view. A legend can be placed on several sheets.

A legend view

A type dragged from Families in the Project Index into a legend becomes its legend component where it is dropped; a type of Families ▸ Symbols places that annotation symbol. Create Same, in the context menu of a selected element, starts the tool that places it with its type: for a legend component, with its view and host length too.

docs.title: Detail lines and regions
docs.text:
Annotations ▸ Detail ▸ Detail line (DL) draws lines in the open view only, in the line style of the Line style panel. The Draw panel offers Line, Rectangle, Inscribed Polygon, Circumscribed Polygon, Circle, Start-End-Radius Arc, Center-ends Arc, Tangent End Arc, Spline, Ellipse, Partial Ellipse and Fillet Arc. The options bar shows what the shape takes:

The Draw group Option What it does Continue Each line (or arc, or spline) starts where the last ended; off, each one stands alone Offset What is drawn moves that far sideways; chained lines join at their corners Radius A circle, polygon or centre-ends arc of that radius (a circle takes one click); chained lines and rectangles get round corners. Offset is then ignored Sides The number of sides of a polygon

After the first click, type a length (a line, a chord) or a radius (circles, polygons, arcs, ellipse axes) and press Enter; the value shows at the cursor. A centre-ends arc never exceeds 180°: past it, it turns the other way, and a typed angle sets its end. A tangent arc starts at the end of a line or arc you click. Shift keeps lines and polygon radii horizontal or vertical and turns chords, arc radii and ellipse axes in steps of 45°, and keeps the sweep of an arc at 90°, 180° or 270°. Esc ends a chain or a spline. The same shapes and options are in every sketch (floors, roofs, filled regions, revision clouds, wall boundaries).

Pick Lines makes a detail line on a wall's face, axis or layer, a grid or another line under the cursor (Tab for the next one), moved by Offset; with Lock the line stays on it and follows when it moves. Fillet Arc picks two lines and rounds their corner, with the arc under the cursor or of the Radius set. A selected detail line has grips at its ends and a temporary dimension of its length: type a value to change it. The end of a line selected on its own drags alone and leaves the next line where it is; with a chain selected (Tab), the ends where its lines meet drag together, in one undo step. The cursor snaps to the ends, middles, centres and crossings of the view's detail lines.

Filled region ▸ Filled region opens sketch mode: the boundary is sketched with every shape of the Draw panel and with Pick Lines, and loops inside another are holes. Curves are kept as short straight segments. Esc ends a chain and keeps the sketch; Modify and the Modify tools work on its lines. Finish Edit Mode makes the region in the current region type, or says why it cannot (an open or crossing boundary). A selected region's Edit Boundary opens its sketch again. The type sets its fill pattern, colour and background (Opaque hides what is behind). Filled region ▸ Masking Region makes a region in the paper colour that hides what is beneath it. A region shows its Area and has Comments. A selected region has a grip at each vertex: drag one to change its shape.

Filled regions, detail lines and a masking region

docs.title: Detail components, repeating details and insulation
docs.text:
• Component ▸ Detail component: a 2D symbol (brick, block, timber, steel section, insulation board, break line) placed in a drafting or detail view; the space bar lines it up with each wall or detail line near the cursor in turn (a quarter turn when there is none).
  • Component ▸ Repeating detail: click a start and an end; the type sets the repeated component, the Layout (fill the available space, fixed distance, fixed number, maximum spacing), the Spacing, Inside and the rotation within the pattern. The instance has the Number when the layout is a fixed number.
  • Insulation: click two points; Width and Offset (the insulation runs that far to the left of the clicks) in the options bar; with Pick Lines ticked, a click on a detail line or a wall draws it along that line. The insulation width and the bulge ratio in its properties. Selected insulation, and a selected repeating detail, have a grip at each end.
A wall detail in a free 2D view

docs.title: Draw order
docs.text: Select detail items only: Arrange offers Bring to Front, Bring Forward, Send to Back and Send Backward. Detail items always draw over the model, and a new one goes on top. Undo restores the previous order.

docs.title: Free 2D views
docs.text:
Views ▸ Create ▸ Free 2D View asks for a name and a scale (or a custom one). The view opens and is listed under Free 2D Views; everything drawn in it is 2D, with no model behind it. It can go on one sheet. Duplicate View ▸ Duplicate with Detailing copies a view with its detail items, text, dimensions and legend components.

Display Model in the properties of a plan, a section or a detail view draws the model Normal, Halftone (greyed under the details) or not at all (Do not display), leaving the details and annotations.

Views ▸ Create ▸ Detail with Reference other view ticked on the options bar draws a callout that points at an existing detail or free 2D view instead of making a new one: its head names that view and a double-click opens it; Referenced view in its properties changes it. In a free 2D view the callout is always of this kind.

Hide at scales coarser than in the properties of a section or a callout hides its symbol in the views whose scale is coarser, for example a 1 : 50 detail left out of the 1 : 100 plan.

docs.title: At the command line
docs.text: Every tool has its command: dim, lineardim, angulardim, radialdim, arcdim, spotelevation, text, findreplace, tag, room, roomsep, areaplan, areaboundary, area, colorscheme, legend, legendview, legendcomponent, detailline, region, mask, draworder, lock, eq. help followed by a command shows its usage; Keyboard shortcuts lists the typed shortcuts.

docs.title: Command line and MCP
docs.text: Everything you do in BIMopen is a command. A click on Wall and two points in the plan run the same wall command you can type yourself. This chapter describes the command line of the window, the bimopen-cli program, which runs the same commands without a window, and the MCP server, through which an AI agent can model, check and render a project.

docs.title: The command line in the window
docs.text:
The command line sits under the drawing area. Its upper part is the log; its last row is where you type.

  • You do not need to click it first: whatever you type while no other field is being edited goes there.
  • Enter runs the line. The command is echoed in the log after a >, followed by its result; an error is shown in red and changes nothing.
  • Up and Down bring back the lines typed before.
  • On the left of the row, the prompt says what is expected: Command: when no tool is active, or the request of the active tool, such as WALL next point [Esc to finish]:.
  • help lists every command with a line of description; help wall shows the usage of one. ? ▸ Commands in the top bar does the same as help.

docs.title: Typed shortcuts start the tools
docs.text:
A command typed without arguments starts the interactive tool, as if you clicked its button: WA (or wall) starts the wall tool, DR the door tool, VG opens Visibility and Graphics. The same command with arguments does the work at once, without the tool: wall 0,0 5,0 draws a wall from the origin to 5 m along x.

Command names, their short forms and their arguments are the same in every language of the interface; most also accept an Italian name, such as muro for wall. Parameter names, type names and view names follow the language of the interface: in English you type set Free Height 2.7m, in Italian set Altezza libera 2.7m. The keyboard shortcuts chapter lists every short form.

docs.title: Points and lengths
docs.text:
You type It means 3,4 The point x = 3 m, y = 4 m @2,0 2 m along x and 0 along y from the previous point @4<90 4 m from the previous point, at 90° (angles counter-clockwise from the x axis) 2.7m, 270cm, 2700mm A length with its unit 2.7 or 2,7 A length in metres: at the command line a number without unit is in metres

For example, wall 0,0 @6,0 @4<90 0,4 c draws a 6 × 4 m rectangle; the final c closes it.

Warning

At the command line set Free Height 2700 means 2700 metres. Write the unit: 2700mm. In the element panel, instead, a number without unit is in the project's units, millimetres in a new project.

docs.title: Arguments in JSON
docs.text:
Every command also takes its arguments as a JSON object, which gives access to all its options. The usage line of help lists them:

wall 0,0 10,0 {"height":3.2,"location":"Linea d'asse del muro"}
roof walls {"slope":30,"overhang":0.5}
sheet A102 Plans {"title_block":"A3"}
export doors.csv {"schedule":"doors"}

docs.title: Commands you will use often
docs.text:
Command What it does new, sample A new project, the sample project open house.bimopen, save house.bimopen Opens and saves a project undo, redo Undoes and redoes the last change view 3d, view Ground Floor Opens the default 3D view, or the plan of a level wall, door, window, floor, roof Model elements: see the usage with help select walls, select all, deselect Selects by category, everything, nothing set <parameter> <value> Sets a parameter of the selection, as in the element panel type <type name> Changes the type of the selection, or of the next element move 1,0, copy 0,3, rotate 90 Modifies the selection delete Deletes the selection list walls, params 102, info Lists elements, the parameters of one, a summary of the project schedule doors Shows a schedule at the command line export house.ifc Exports IFC, SVG, PNG or CSV, by the file's extension

Every element has a number, its id, shown in brackets after it is created: Door «Single swing door 80x210» in wall 102 (106). Commands accept it where they need an element: params 106, delete 106.

docs.title: bimopen-cli
docs.text:
bimopen-cli runs BIMopen without a window: to convert files, to build a project from a script, to check a model, or to serve agents over MCP. Build it with cargo build --release -p bimopen-cli.

bimopen-cli info <file>
bimopen-cli convert <in> <out> [--level NAME] [--view 3d] [--schedule walls|doors|windows|floors|rooms|materials]
bimopen-cli run [<file> | --sample] [--cmd LINE]… [--script FILE] [--save FILE] [--export FILE]…
bimopen-cli commands
bimopen-cli mcp [<file> | --sample]
Subcommand What it does info <file> A summary of the project and, in JSON, its levels, element counts and active view convert <in> <out> Opens <in> (.bimopen or .rvt) and writes <out>: .ifc, .svg or .png of a plan (the lowest level, or --level), .png of the 3D view (--view 3d), .csv of a schedule (--schedule), or .bimopen run Opens a file, the sample, or a new project, then runs the options in order: --cmd one line, --script a file of lines (empty lines and lines starting with # are skipped), --save and --export a file commands Every command, with its description and usage mcp The MCP server on standard input and output --version The version

The messages are in the language of the environment variable BIMOPEN_LANG (it, en, de, fr, es, ar), or of the system (LANG), or Italian. bimopen-cli ends with code 0 when everything worked, 1 when a command failed (the message says which), and 2 when the arguments are wrong (it prints the usage).

export BIMOPEN_LANG=en
bimopen-cli run --script house.txt --save house.bimopen --export house.ifc
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen plan.svg
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen doors.csv --schedule doors
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen first.png --level "First Floor"
bimopen-cli convert house.bimopen house-3d.png --view 3d
bimopen-cli convert project.rvt project.bimopen

A script is a text file with one command per line, exactly as typed at the command line:

# a small house
wall 0,0 10,0 10,6 0,6 c
door 5,0
window 10,3
floor walls
roof walls

The schedules are written as CSV with ; between the columns, the headings in the language of the messages and a total row at the end.

docs.title: MCP: BIMopen for AI agents
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI agent use programs as tools. bimopen-cli mcp is an MCP server: it speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 on standard input and output, one message per line, and keeps one project open for the whole conversation. Without a file it starts from a new project; --sample starts from the sample house.

To add it to an agent, give the agent the command to start. For example, in Claude Code:

claude mcp add bimopen -- bimopen-cli mcp --sample

or, in a client configured with JSON:

{ "mcpServers": { "bimopen": { "command": "bimopen-cli", "args": ["mcp", "--sample"] } } }

The server offers seven tools:

Tool Arguments What it does command_line line Types a line at the command line, exactly as a person would execute command, args Runs a command with its arguments in JSON inspect_model – A summary: levels, element counts, active view, selection query_elements category (optional) The elements, with id, category and name: walls, doors, windows, floors, rooms, roomseps, grids, levels, types get_params id Every parameter of an element schedule kind A schedule: walls, doors, windows, floors, rooms or materials render view, width, height, yaw, pitch A PNG image of a view: 3d, the name of a level for its plan, of a section, elevation, callout or free 2D view, or the number or name of a sheet; yaw and pitch turn the 3D camera, in degrees

The answers carry the message of the command and, when there is one, its data in JSON, such as the ids of the elements created. An agent can check its own work by asking for a render.

Tip

Ask the agent to render the plan and the 3D view after each step: it sees what it built and corrects itself.

docs.title: Sheets, schedules and printing
docs.text: This chapter describes how the project is documented: sheets and their title blocks, the views placed on them, revisions, schedules, printed drawings and exported images.

docs.title: Sheets
docs.text:
A sheet is a drawing to print: a title block and the views placed on it. Sheets are listed under Sheets (all) in the Project Index, by number.

A sheet with both floor plans, and the Document tools on the rail

docs.title: Creating a sheet
docs.text:
Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Sheet opens New Sheet: choose a title block (its paper size is shown), None, or one of the placeholder sheets of the sheet list. OK creates the sheet with the next free number (A101, A102…) and opens it.

New Sheet

Right-click a sheet in the Project Index ➤ Rename… to change its number and name in Sheet Title. The other parameters of the sheet are in the element panel: Sheet Number, Sheet Name, Sheet Issue Date, Drawn By, Checked By, Designed By, Approved By, Appears In Sheet List, its guide grid and its revisions. Several sheets picked together in the Project Index (with Ctrl or Shift) are changed together: the panel shows the values they share.

Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Project information sets what every sheet shows: Project Issue Date, Project Status, Client Name, Project Address, Project Name and Project Number.

Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Note Block makes a schedule of the symbols placed with Symbol, of one family only (north arrows, targets, revision deltas…): in New Note Block choose the Family and type the Note Block Name, then OK. Note Block Properties opens first, with the same tabs as any schedule; by default each row shows the symbol's type, its text and the count.

docs.title: Title blocks
docs.text:
The title block shows the project's information, the sheet's number and name, the people and the dates, the current revision and the scale (As indicated when the views have different scales); above it, a table lists the sheet's revisions with their number, description and date. A double click on one of its fields types the value in place.

  • Click a line of the title block to pick it: the type selector changes it to another paper size, Del removes it (the sheet and its views stay).
  • Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Title Block inserts one on the open sheet: choose it in the type selector, its frame follows the cursor, click to place it.
  • Type Parameters shows its Sheet width and Sheet height; Duplicate… makes a new paper size.

docs.title: Views on sheets
docs.text:
Drag a view from the Project Index onto the sheet, or use Document ➤ Sheets ➤ View (Views, then Add View to Sheet): the view follows the cursor at its scale, and a click places it as a viewport. A view goes on one sheet only; a schedule on several.

A picked viewport:

  • moves with the mouse or the arrow keys, unless it is pinned (Fix); near another view, its title lines up with the other's and a dashed line shows it;
  • has its View Scale, its Title on Sheet (also typed by double-clicking the title) and its Rotation on Sheet (90° clockwise or counter-clockwise; the title stays horizontal);
  • shows the end of its title line, which can be dragged;
  • takes a viewport type from the type selector: No Title, Title w/ Line or Title w/o Line, or a type of your own (Show Title, Show Extension Line, line weight, colour and pattern of the line);
  • leaves the sheet with Del; the view stays in the project.
A viewport picked on a sheet

Activate View (on the Selection: Viewports card or the right button) edits the view where it is on the sheet, the rest of the sheet in halftone; Deactivate View goes back to the sheet. A view turned on its sheet cannot be activated: take its rotation off first. A double click on a view opens it in its own window.

docs.title: Guide grids
docs.text: Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Guide Grid asks for a name and covers the sheet with a grid. Pick it to drag its corners or to set its Guide spacing; the sheet's Guide Grid parameter shows the same grid on other sheets, or none. Views dragged near the grid's lines snap onto them. The grid is never printed.

docs.title: Sheet list
docs.text: Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Sheet List makes a schedule of the sheets: number, name and any other field. Sheets with Appears In Sheet List unticked are left out. Rows ➤ New adds a placeholder sheet: a row that is not a sheet yet and is not in the Project Index. Filter placeholder sheets shows every row, hides the placeholders or shows only them. A placeholder chosen in New Sheet becomes a real sheet.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
Document ➤ Sheets ➤ Sheet Issues/Revisions lists the revisions of the project, one per row: Sequence, Numbering (Numeric, Alphabetic or none), Date, Description, Issued, Issued to, Issued by and Show. Add adds one; a row picked by its sequence number is merged into the one above or below (its clouds go with it) or moved up and down. Numbering is Per Project or Per Sheet (the place of the revision among the sheet's revisions); Alphabetical order ➤ Options… sets the letters used. An issued revision cannot be changed, and neither can its clouds, until Issued is unticked.

Document ➤ Detail ➤ Revision Cloud draws a cloud in a plan, a section, a free 2D view or on a sheet: sketch closed loops with the shapes of the Draw group, then Finish Edit Mode; a selected cloud's Edit Sketch opens them again, unless its revision is issued. The cloud takes the latest revision not issued; picked, it shows its Revision (to change), its number, date and people, its Mark and Comments. Show of a revision draws its clouds and tags, keeps them but does not draw them, or hides them.

A sheet lists the revisions of the clouds of its views and of its own clouds. Its Revisions on Sheet (in the element panel, Edit…) adds other revisions to the list.

docs.title: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule is a table of the elements of the model, and a view like the others: it opens in a window of the drawing area, is tiled, cascaded and switched with plans, sections and 3D views, and is listed under Schedules/Quantities in the Project Index. It follows every change of the model at once, and every change made in it changes the model.

Schedules beside the plan, selected together

docs.title: Creating a schedule
docs.text: Views ➤ Create ➤ Schedules ➤ Schedule/Quantities opens New Schedule: choose a category, a name (the default follows the category until one is typed) and Schedule building components or Schedule keys. OK opens Schedule Properties; its second OK creates the schedule and opens its view. Material Takeoff in the same menu lists the materials of the layers of walls, floors and roofs.

docs.title: Schedule Properties
docs.text:
The dialog opens again from the element panel of the schedule (each tab has its Edit… button) or from the right button on the schedule in the Project Index. Its tabs:

Tab What it sets Fields The columns, chosen from Available fields: and put in order; the fields of the rooms the elements are in; Add Parameter… for a project or shared parameter; Calculated Value… for a formula (with + - * / ^, sqrt, round, IF, AND, OR, NOT and units) or a percentage Filter Up to four criteria, all of which an element must meet Sorting/Grouping Up to four sort levels, each with Header, footer and Blank line; the grand totals; Itemize every instance (off: one row per type) Formatting Per field: heading, orientation, alignment, hidden field, Format… (units, rounding, symbol), totals and Conditional Format… (a background colour where a value meets a test) Appearance Grid lines and outline with their line styles, the title and the column headers, a blank row, Header text and Body text (size, Bold, Italic); shown when the schedule is on a sheet

docs.title: Working in a schedule view
docs.text:
• A cell edits the element, or its type for a type parameter; every edit is one step of undo.
  • A row selects its elements in every view. Highlight in model on the Edit | Schedule/Quantities card opens Show Elements in View, which brings a plan forward framed on them; Show goes on to the next view.
  • Rows ➤ Delete deletes the elements of the selected rows, after asking.
  • Headings picked together are joined under a common heading with Group, and parted with Ungroup; Hide column and Unhide all columns work on the column picked.

docs.title: Schedules on sheets
docs.text:
Drag a schedule from the Project Index onto a sheet. Selected on the sheet, it shows its controls: the Z on the right edge of a segment splits it in two, the arrow in the middle of a segment moves it (dropped on the segment beside it, the two join), the dot at the bottom of a segment moves its last row, and the triangles at the top of the columns set their widths. A double click, or Edit Schedule on the right button, opens the schedule view. The same schedule can go on several sheets.

A schedule on a sheet, with its controls

docs.title: Key schedules and material takeoffs
docs.text:
A key schedule (Schedule keys in New Schedule) defines named sets of values, one row per key, added and deleted with Rows. Its Key Name becomes a parameter of the category: choosing a key for an element gives it all the values of that row.

A material takeoff lists, for each element, the materials of its layers with their area and volume; its fields can be sorted, grouped and totalled like any other.

docs.title: Project and shared parameters
docs.text:
Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Project Parameters adds parameters to the elements of some categories, or to their types, with a name, a type of value and the group they show in the element panel.

Settings ➤ Settings ➤ Shared Parameters opens Edit Shared Parameters: the shared parameter file in use (Browse…, Create…), its groups and the parameters of each group. A shared parameter keeps its name and type, and has an identifier of its own, so that several projects add the same parameter. In Parameter Properties, choose Shared parameter and Select… to add one to the project; Export… writes a shared parameter of the project back to the file.

docs.title: Exporting and reusing schedules
docs.text:
• Application menu ➤ Export ➤ Reports ➤ Schedule… writes the schedule as delimited text: Export Schedule sets the field delimiter, the text qualifier and which headings and group rows go in the file.
  • Create view template from view… on the right button of a schedule makes a view template with its fields, filter, sorting, formatting and appearance; Apply view template… gives them to another schedule.
  • Save to New File… on the right button writes the schedule's setup, without the elements, to a file of its own. Create ➤ Load from library ➤ Insert from File ➤ Insert Views from File… brings the schedules of another project into this one, with their project parameters.

docs.title: Printing
docs.text: Printing writes PDF files: on the desktop they are saved where you choose, in the browser they are downloaded.

docs.title: The Print dialog
docs.text:
Ctrl+P, or application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print…, opens Print:

  • File: the name of the file and, when several views or sheets are printed, Combine multiple selected views/sheets into a single file (one page each) or Create separate files (one file each, named after the sheet or view).
  • Print Range: Current window, Visible portion of current window (only what the window shows), or Selected views/sheets with Select….
  • Reverse print order prints the last page first.
  • Settings: the print settings in use, changed with Settings…; Preview shows the pages.
Print

Plans, sections, elevations, free 2D views and sheets print as drawings; the 3D window prints as an image of the view; a schedule prints its table on a page. The page is always white, elements hidden temporarily in a window are printed, and each printed sheet carries the date and time of the print.

docs.title: View/sheet sets
docs.text: Select… opens View/Sheet Set: tick the sheets and views to print (Show sheets, views or both; Check all, Check none). A set is saved by name with Save As… and kept in the project; Save, Reset, Rename… and Delete manage the saved sets, and the name list picks one again.

docs.title: Print Setup
docs.text:
application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print Setup…, or Settings… in Print, sets:

Setting What it does Size and Orientation The paper (A0 to A4, or the sheet's own size) and its orientation Paper Placement Center, or an offset from the lower-left corner Hidden line views Vector Processing (sections and elevations print only the lines that are seen: the lines behind nearer surfaces are removed, not just covered, and lines lying on one another print once, so the PDF opens clean in other programs) or Raster Processing (the pages as images, at the raster quality chosen) Zoom Fit to page, or a percentage of the real size Colors Black Lines, Grayscale or Colour Options Show view links in blue, Hide unreferenced view tags, Hide crop boundaries, Replace halftone with thin lines, Keep coincident lines (off: two lines lying on one another in printed and exported sections and elevations become one; on: both stay, each with its own element) Print Setup

Settings are saved by name with Save As…, and kept in the project. Closing the dialog after changing saved settings asks whether to save the changes; No keeps them for this session only.

docs.title: Print Preview
docs.text: application menu ➤ Print ➤ Print Preview, or Preview in Print, shows the pages as they will print, in their colours: Previous Page and Next Page go through them, the wheel zooms and dragging pans; Print… prints, Close goes back.

docs.title: Exporting images
docs.text:
application menu ➤ Export ➤ Images and animations ➤ Image… opens Export Image:

  • the file name and the Export Range: the current window, its visible portion, or the views and sheets chosen (one file each);
  • the Image Size: Fit view(s)/sheet(s) to a number of pixels across or down, or a zoom percentage of the real size at a resolution;
  • the options, as for printing: view links in blue, crop boundaries and unreferenced view tags hidden;
  • the Format of views without shading and of shaded views: PNG, JPEG, BMP or TIFF.

The 3D window is exported as it is shown, with its graphic style.

docs.title: Floors, roofs, stairs and components
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs and railings are drawn in sketch mode: their lines are sketched first, and the element is made only when the sketch is finished. Components (furniture and plumbing fixtures) are placed with a click. Curtain walls are described in Walls, doors and windows.

docs.title: Sketch mode
docs.text:
Create ▸ Build ▸ Flooring, Roof, Stairs and Railing open sketch mode. The contextual card is named after what is sketched (Edit | Create Floor Boundary, Create Roof Footprint, Create Stairs Sketch, Create Railing Path) and has:

  • the Mode group: Finish Edit Mode makes the element; Cancel Edit Mode drops the sketch and leaves the model as it was;
  • the Draw group, with the drawing tools of the element;
  • for stairs and railings, the Tools group.
Sketch mode: the contextual card and the magenta lines

Nothing is made while sketching: the lines are magenta, and the model changes only with Finish Edit Mode. The whole element is then one step of the undo history: one Ctrl+Z takes it away.

docs.title: Drawing lines
docs.text:
Tool How it draws Line Click point after point: each click ends a line and starts the next. The length and angle of the line under the cursor are shown beside it; Shift keeps it horizontal or vertical. With Continue off on the options strip, each line is drawn on its own. Clicking the start of the chain again closes the loop Type a length and press Enter: the line ends that far along the cursor's direction (a stair's run too). Rectangle Two opposite corners: four lines Pick Walls Click a wall: its line is added to the sketch (see below). Press Tab over a wall, then click, to pick the whole chain of walls joined end to end Pick Lines Move over a wall, a grid, a line or the edge of a floor or roof: the line under the cursor is highlighted and named (a wall's faces, each layer boundary, its two Core Boundary lines and its axis); Tab goes to the next one there. Click to add a sketch line on it (set off by Offset towards the cursor) Slope Arrow Click the tail, then the head of the arrow (floors and roofs)

Offset on the options strip moves the drawn lines (and the lines of picked walls) by that distance.

The arcs of the Draw group (and a circle, as two halves) are one sketch line each: picked, measured and dragged as arcs, kept by the floor, roof, stair, wall boundary or filled region, and given back as arcs by Edit Boundary or Edit Sketch. In every view a sketch point snaps to the ends and middles of the sketch's lines and arcs, to arcs' centres, where lines cross and onto a line or an arc; from the point being drawn from, to the foot of a perpendicular and to the point where a line touches an arc. The marker and its name show where the point snaps; S C and S P ask for the centre or the perpendicular for the next point.

Floors and roofs need closed loops. A loop drawn inside the outer one is an opening: the floor or the roof has a hole there. When Finish Edit Mode finds lines that do not close or that cross, a message says so and the sketch stays open to be fixed (Continue).

docs.title: Picking and changing sketch lines
docs.text:
Esc ends the chain being drawn; a second Esc puts the drawing tool down (so does Modify). While the sketch is open its lines are elements of the view, and Modify works on them as on other lines; nothing else can be picked until the sketch is finished:

  • the line under the cursor is highlighted; a click selects it, Ctrl adds lines, Shift takes them away, a window selects several, Tab the chain of joined lines;
  • the end of a line selected on its own drags alone: the line next to it stays where it is and the join is broken; with a chain selected (Tab), the ends where its lines meet drag together; a dragged line takes the lines joined to it along;
  • Move, Copy, Rotate, Mirror on Line, Repeat in Series, Align, Offset, Shorten/Lengthen and Split Element work on them, and the sketch stays open;
  • one selected line shows temporary dimensions to the nearest parallel line on each side (another sketch line, the wall's original outline, a wall, a grid, a level): click the value and type a distance to move the line; the symbol beside it makes a permanent dimension, kept while the sketch is open;
  • its properties are in the element panel: Defines Slope and Slope, for a roof line picked from a wall its Overhang, and its Length.

Align takes as its reference the line under the cursor, and Tab goes to the next one there, so a sketch line can be aligned to a wall's layer or core boundary. While drawing or dragging an end, the points snap to the corners of the walls' faces, layers and core boundaries, then onto those lines. Del deletes the selected lines. Ctrl+Z while sketching takes back the last change to the sketch, not to the model. All this works in plans, in sections and elevations (a wall's boundary) and, for selecting, dragging ends and deleting, in the 3D view.

docs.title: Editing the sketch of an element
docs.text:
Select a floor, a roof, a stair or a railing: the Mode group of its contextual card has Edit Boundary (floors), Edit Footprint (roofs), Edit Sketch (stairs) or Edit Path (railings). Sketch mode opens with the element's lines, openings, slopes and arrow; Finish Edit Mode changes the same element, Cancel Edit Mode leaves it unchanged.

The sketch opens with Modify active: its lines can be selected and changed at once.

In a plan the sketch is drawn on the level; in the 3D view it lies on the element's own plane (the floor's top, the roof's base) and the 3D view stays open.

A new floor can be sketched in the 3D view too: Flooring started there puts the sketch on the plane of the level, the line being drawn follows the cursor with its length, and Finish Edit Mode makes the floor without leaving the 3D view. In the 3D view the options strip's Level chooses the work plane: the level whose plane the sketch lies on and the floor goes on. Pick Walls takes the wall whose face is under the cursor. Roofs by footprint, stairs and railings are sketched in a plan.

docs.title: Floors
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Flooring. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls.
  2. Click the walls around the floor, or press Tab over one of them and click to pick them all. Each line goes on the interior face of its wall; the lines of walls that meet are trimmed or extended to meet at the corner.
  3. Or draw the boundary with Line or Rectangle; draw a loop inside it for an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.
A floor: TAB on the walls, click, Finish Edit Mode

On the options strip, Extend into wall (to core) puts picked lines into the wall up to the face of its core, and Offset moves them (a negative offset moves them away from the walls). The type of the new floor is the one in the type selector at the top of Properties.

docs.title: Sloped floors
docs.text:
A floor slopes in one direction, set in one of two ways while sketching:

  • a Slope Arrow: its properties are Specify (Height at Tail, from the heights of its two ends, or Slope), Height Offset at Tail, Height Offset at Head and Slope. The heights are measured from the top of the floor;
  • one boundary line with Defines Slope ticked and its Slope in degrees: the floor rises from that line, inwards.

The floor is sloped in 3D and in sections. Its Slope Angle in Properties changes the slope afterwards.

docs.title: Floors over walls
docs.text: When a floor crosses walls (an upper floor resting on the walls below, for instance), its slab is cut out of them: in 3D and in sections the wall stops under the floor and goes on above it, and walls go on through the floor's openings.

docs.title: Floor properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Level, Height Offset From Level The level and the height of the top face from it Slope Angle The slope of a sloped floor, in degrees Thickness From the type's layers (read-only) Perimeter, Area, Volume Without the openings (read-only) Comments, Mark Free text The properties of a floor

Type Parameters has the floor's Structure (its layers) and its default thickness.

docs.title: Roofs
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Roof. Sketch mode starts with Pick Walls; the options strip has Defines Slope, Overhang and Extend into wall (to core).
  2. Pick the walls (Tab for the whole chain). Each line goes on the exterior face of its wall, moved out by the overhang (from the face of the core with Extend into wall (to core)).
  3. Or draw the footprint with Line or Rectangle; a loop inside is an opening.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.
A roof: the footprint, then the roof

Every line with Defines Slope rises inwards at its Slope (30° by default); a small triangle with the slope is drawn beside it. The shape comes from those lines:

  • all the lines define the slope: a hip roof;
  • two opposite lines do not: a gable roof, the walls under the gables rise to the ridge when attached;
  • no line defines the slope: a flat roof, or a roof sloping along a Slope Arrow (then no line may define a slope).
Hip, gable and flat

To change one line, press Esc twice, click the line and change Defines Roof Slope, Slope or (lines picked from walls) Overhang in Properties.

Select walls, click Modify Wall ▸ Link Top/Base, then the roof: they rise to its underside, gables included (Walls, doors and windows tells more).

docs.title: Roof properties
docs.text:
Property What it is Base Level, Base Offset From Level Where the eaves are: by default on top of the walls of the level Slope The slope of every line that defines one (or of the arrow) Thickness, Maximum Ridge Height, Area, Volume Read-only Comments, Mark Free text

In plan a roof shows its outline, ridges and hips; in 3D its slopes, overhangs and layers.

docs.title: Stairs
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Stairs. Sketch mode starts with Run.
  2. Click where the first riser is, then where the run ends: the run snaps to whole treads, and the status bar counts the risers made and left (for example 9 risers created, 8 remaining).
  3. To turn, click again away from the end of the first run and draw the next one: a landing joins them. At any angle the landing is bounded by the two runs' risers, its outer corner where their outer sides meet.
  4. When every riser is placed, click Finish Edit Mode.
A stair by runs: the count of risers made and left

Dashed guides show where the next run can start: the last run's extension beyond its end and the lines of its first and last risers. A click near them snaps onto them. In a 3D view the stair is drawn the same way, on the plane of the active level.

A curved run (a spiral stair): with Run active, click Center-ends arc, then the centre, the start of the run line (its distance from the centre is the radius of the walking line) and the end, going round past half a turn if needed, but under one turn (further, the run stops short and the status bar warns that the runs would overlap). The risers radiate from the centre a tread apart on the run line; riser lines drawn radiating from a centre make a curved run too. A second curved run round the same centre and on the same run line (a click near them takes them) is joined to the first by a landing along the arc.

A stair can also be drawn by its lines. In its sketch, click Draw ▸ Boundary and draw the left and right edges (green), then Riser and draw the riser lines (black) between them, with Line or Pick Lines. Parallel, evenly spaced risers make a run, as wide as the risers; a landing joins two runs out to the boundary lines. Each riser is as high as the storey divided by the desired number of risers; with fewer riser lines the stair stops short of the top (Properties shows the actual number). Edit Sketch gives the same lines back. Each run drawn with Run is at once boundary and riser lines like these: they can be moved or deleted like the others. A landing follows its boundary lines: split its far edge with Split Element and drag a piece to notch it, or draw it wider than the runs.

The Width on the options strip is that of the new stair (by default the type's). Tools ▸ Railing Type chooses the railings of the new stair: a railing type, put on both sides, or None.

The number of risers comes from the height between Base Level and Top Level (with their offsets) and the type's Maximum Riser Height; changing a level or an offset in Properties changes the risers. Edit Sketch reopens its boundary and riser lines: change or delete them (click, Del) and draw runs again; the railings of the stair follow. Multistory Top Level repeats the stair, with its railings, storey by storey up to that level; a storey whose height is not the stair's gets no copy, and a warning names it. With the stair selected, the blue flip arrows beside its first riser make it go up from the other end; Up Label, Up Arrow, Down Label and Down Arrow in Properties show or hide the plan symbol's parts. The square grip under the UP text drags it elsewhere.

In plan the stair shows its treads up to the cut line, the break line, the arrow and the UP/DN text; in 3D its treads and risers, or a monolithic slab, its landings and railings.

A stair in plan

docs.title: How a stair is built
docs.text:
Type Parameters of the stair decide its construction:

  • Monolithic Stairs ticked: each run is a concrete slab cut to the steps; its underside runs parallel to the slope, Structural Depth below the inner corners of the steps, and the landings are as thick: the sloping underside of a run meets the landing's underside along a line, without a step; each run ends with its last tread: the landing, flush with it, or the floor above makes the last riser, so steps and slab show as one solid with no line across the risers.
  • otherwise treads (Tread Thickness) with risers (Riser Type Straight, Riser Thickness) or open (None), on stringers: Right Stringer and Left Stringer Closed (a board the treads are housed in), Open (a board cut to the steps, the treads on top) or None, and Middle Stringers under the treads, with their Stringer Thickness and Stringer Height.
  • Begin with Riser and End with Riser cleared: the board of the stair's first or last riser is not built.
  • Riser Type Slanted leans each riser board, its top under the front of the tread above; Riser to Tread Connection runs each tread under the riser behind it (Extend Tread Under Riser) or the riser down behind the tread (Extend Riser Behind Tread).
  • Nosing Length sets how far a tread runs past its riser; Extend Below Base moves the foot of the stringers (negative: below the base level); Tread Material, Riser Material, Stringer Material and Monolithic Material colour the parts; Break Symbol in Plan and Text Size control the plan symbol.
The type parameters of a stair

The landing stops behind the last riser of the run that reaches it, following its back face; in a monolithic stair it starts at the riser's face. In a monolithic stair whose top floor has its edge on the last riser, the run's underside goes on under that floor until it meets the floor's underside, as under a landing.

A section across the stair shows it cut with its slab. Volume in Properties and in the schedule of stairs is the volume of its solids.

The type's Text Font, Nosing Profile (Default or Rounded) and Apply Nosing Profile (front only, front and left, or front, left and right: past a side without a closed stringer), Open Stringer Offset, Trim Stringers at Top (Match Level stops the side stringers at the top level) and its identification (Code, Model, Manufacturer, Type Comments, URL, Description, Assembly Code) are in Type Parameters, as is a monolithic stair's Underside of Stringer (Smooth, a sloping slab, or Stepped: the slab follows the steps). Under Calculation Rules, Use Stair Calculator with a Target, Maximum and Minimum Result checks 2 risers + 1 tread: a stair outside the range is made, and a warning says so.

docs.title: Ramps
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Ramp. Sketch mode starts with Run.
  2. Click where a run starts, then where it ends: it slopes at most the type's Ramp Max Slope (1/x) and rises at most its Maximum Incline Length (while drawing, a longer run stops there); the length made and left show beside the cursor.
  3. Draw the next run away from the end of the first: a landing joins them. Boundary and Riser draw a ramp by its lines, with a riser line at the start and the end of each run.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

The type's Shape is Thick (its Thickness) or Solid (down to the base), and Ramp Material colours it. Its railings, Edit Sketch and Properties work as for stairs.

With Arc from Center and End in the Draw group, click the centre, the start of the run line and then its end round the centre: the run curves round it, two lines radiating from the centre at its ends and two boundary arcs at its sides. The type's Show Up Arrow in All Views draws the whole up arrow and UP in the plan of the top level too; its Text Font and identification are as for stairs.

docs.title: Railings
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Railing.
  2. Draw the path with Line: one chain of connected lines (a path in pieces, a closed path or one that goes back over itself is refused at Finish Edit Mode).
  3. To put the railing on a stair, click Tools ▸ Pick New Host and then the stair: the path drawn on it climbs with the stair.
  4. Click Finish Edit Mode.

Edit Path reopens a railing's path. Create ▸ Vertical Links ▸ Railing ▸ Place on a host puts a railing on each side of the stair or ramp you click: on the options bar Position chooses On treads (on the stair's edge) or On stringer (over the stringer, where the stair has one), Offset from Path moves it towards the inside of the stair and Invert switches between the two positions. The same two values are in the Properties of a stair's railing.

The railing's Type Parameters hold for every railing of that type: Railing Height (that of the top rail), Baluster Spacing, Baluster Offset (balusters and posts moved sideways) and the identity data; the preview shows the railing on a sample stair, seen from the side. Rail Structure (Non-Continuous) ▸ Edit… opens the list of the rails below the top one (Name, Height above the walking surface, Offset sideways, a square or round Profile) with Insert, Delete, Up and Down. Baluster Placement ▸ Edit… opens the Main pattern: the baluster or None, where it starts and ends (Host, Top rail or one of the rails) with their offsets, the distance between balusters, Break pattern at (at the end of each segment, at angles greater than a value, or never), Justify, Excess length fill and Use baluster per tread with how many on each tread; and the start, corner and end Posts (the post or None, its offsets, Space along the path, Offset sideways) with Corner posts at. The changes in these two windows apply with OK and are undone with a single Ctrl+Z. The Top rail, Handrail 1 and Handrail 2 rows are greyed: not available yet.

The type parameters of a railing, with the preview

The railings of a stair run on over its landings as one rail, at their height above the line of the nosings and above the landings. Where a run leaves a landing one riser higher, the type's Tangent Joins (the rail goes straight on) and Angled Joins (it turns) decide the join: Extend Rails to Meet (tangent joins only) carries the sloping rail on down to the landing, Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments rises upright at the first riser, No Connector leaves a gap.

The rails are mitred at every joint, where the path turns and where the slope changes: with Rail Connections Weld each rail is one piece, with Trim its pieces are cut on the joint's vertical plane. A post stands at the start and the end of each railing and at every change of direction in plan and wherever the slope changes, as where a run meets a landing. Use Landing Height Adjustment with Landing Height Adjustment raises (or lowers) the rail over the landings by that much.

A stair railing's path follows the stair's outline. Every post stands whole on the tread, landing or floor under it: where it would fall on a riser's line it moves by half its section, so no post sinks into the steps or hangs in front of the first one. Between two posts the balusters are evenly spaced, never wider apart than the spacing.

Place on a host works in plans and in the 3D view: the stair under the cursor shows where the two railings go. On stringer can be chosen only for a stair that has a stringer: on a monolithic stair it is greyed, on the options bar and in Properties. A new railing type has both Angled Joins and Tangent Joins set to Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments, Weld, no landing height adjustment, a bottom rail at 0.100 m (30×30), 20×20 balusters from the bottom rail to the top rail every 0.120 m, broken at the end of each segment and fitted to its length, and 50×50 posts standing on the host: where a run meets a landing the post stands on the landing at the riser's line, with the upright piece of the rail, and nothing runs over the treads. Where the rail rises upright at the start of a run, a low rail stays on the landing without entering the first tread. Edit Joins (one join at a time) is greyed: not available yet.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. Click Create ▸ Build ▸ Component. The type selector lists the components loaded in the project; a preview follows the cursor, in plan and in the 3D view.
  2. Press Space to turn the preview by 90°.
  3. Click to place the component on the level of the plan.
A component follows the cursor before the click

Mode ▸ Load Family opens the library, by folder (Furniture, Plumbing Fixtures): choose a family and click Open to add its types to the project.

Load Family

Select a component and click Host ▸ Pick New Host, then a floor: the component moves onto the floor and stays on its top (click an empty point to put it back on the level). Its properties are Level, Host, Offset from Level, Rotation, Mark and Comments; Type Parameters has its width, depth, height and material.

docs.title: Schedules and IFC
docs.text: Floors, roofs, stairs, railings and furniture have their schedules (Views ▸ Create ▸ Schedules ▸ Schedule/Quantities), one row per element. Export ▸ Export IFC4… writes floors as slabs (with their openings and slopes), roofs, stairs with their flights and landings, railings, furniture and plumbing fixtures. A multistory stair is written once in each storey it is repeated in, with its railings.

docs.title: Not yet in BIMopen
docs.text: Ceilings, roofs by extrusion, shafts and vertical openings, slab edges, fascias, gutters and soffits come after this chapter's realignment.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This chapter shows how to start BIMopen on the desktop and in the browser, what the sample project contains, and how to model a first small house: four walls, a door, a window, a floor, a roof, a 3D view and a sheet with the plan on it. It takes about ten minutes.

docs.title: Running BIMopen on the desktop
docs.text:
BIMopen is built from its source code with Rust, version 1.90 or later. On Linux the graphical interface also needs the development files of xkbcommon, Wayland and GTK 3.

sudo apt-get install -y libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev libgtk-3-dev   # Debian, Ubuntu
cargo run --release -p bimopen -- --sample                             # opens the sample house

The program is bimopen. It accepts a file to open and one option:

Command What it opens bimopen A new, empty project bimopen --sample The sample house bimopen house.bimopen The project saved in house.bimopen bimopen --no-splash As bimopen, without the start screen

You can also open a project by dragging a .bimopen file from the file manager into the window.

docs.title: Start screen
docs.text:
While BIMopen loads, the start screen appears: a window without a frame, centred on the screen, with the name, the version, the loading stage under way with its percentage and a turquoise line growing along the bottom edge. The stages are the real ones (preferences, fonts, graphics card, families, opening the project); the screen stays at least half a second, so it does not flash, and fades out when the main window is ready. It speaks the language chosen in the app, otherwise the system's when it is one of the six, otherwise English.

To leave it out, clear Options ▸ General ▸ Show the start screen (BIMopen remembers it), or start bimopen --no-splash. On Wayland the compositor decides where the window appears (usually in the middle).

docs.title: Language and theme
docs.text:
The first time, BIMopen speaks the language of the operating system when it is one of its six languages (Italian, English, German, French, Spanish, Arabic), and English otherwise. To change it, click the gear at the right end of the top bar (Options) and choose the Language under User Interface. The interface changes at once.

In Options you also choose the Theme, Light or Dark (the sun or the moon in the top bar switches it too), and whether the background of the views is inverted (Invert background color: dark views with light lines). Choosing the dark theme also inverts the background; you can turn it back off. At the first start BIMopen uses the dark theme, with the background inverted. It remembers the language, the theme and the background for the next time.

docs.title: Running BIMopen in the browser
docs.text:
The web version is the same program, compiled for the browser. Open atsanna.github.io/bimopen-site/app/: it starts with the sample house. Nothing needs to be installed, and the project stays in your browser: it is not sent anywhere.

The address accepts these options, which can be combined with &:

Address Effect app/?lang=de Opens in German for this visit (it, en, de, fr, es, ar) app/?empty Starts with a new, empty project instead of the sample app/?webgl Draws with WebGL2 even where WebGPU is available

The browser must support WebGPU or WebGL2. In the browser some things work differently:

  • Open… cannot show a file dialog: drag a .bimopen file into the page to open it;
  • Save and the exports download the file, with the name of the project.

To build the web version yourself:

cargo xtask web                              # builds dist/web
python3 -m http.server 8080 -d dist/web      # then open http://localhost:8080

cargo xtask web needs the wasm32-unknown-unknown target of Rust and the wasm-bindgen command of the version written in Cargo.lock; with binaryen's wasm-opt installed, the result is smaller.

docs.title: The sample project
docs.text:
The sample house shows most of what BIMopen can do. Open it with Application menu ▸ Sample project (the application menu is BIMopen's mark, at the top of the rail), with bimopen --sample, or by typing sample at the command line.

It contains:

  • two levels, each with its floor plan, and five grid lines;
  • fourteen walls of four types, with layers, joined at the corners;
  • six doors and twelve windows, tagged in the plans;
  • two floors, a pitched roof, a stair with its railings and a storefront curtain wall;
  • furniture and plumbing fixtures, eight rooms coloured by use, with a legend;
  • a section, an elevation, an area plan, a saved 3D view and a free 2D view with a wall detail;
  • dimensions, text notes and the schedules of walls, doors, windows, rooms and materials;
  • its place in Cagliari, where its address is: the sun and the shadows are those of that city.

Tip

The sample is a good place to try a tool before using it on your own project: a new sample is always one click away, and nothing you change in it is saved unless you save it.

docs.title: Your first house
